analysis.one_liner: Exempts work performed in an employee's home from federal workplace-safety law.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to committee, and died there without ever getting a vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 so that the law stops applying to any work done in an employee's own residence. That means federal safety standards, employer obligations, and OSHA oversight would no longer cover home offices and other work performed at home, a growing share of work as telecommuting expands. The bill never advanced: it had zero cosponsors, was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, and received no further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers with home-based or telecommuting employees. They would no longer face OSHA requirements, inspections, or enforcement tied to work performed in employees' homes, and would not be responsible for safety conditions in a residence they do not control.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision to the OSH Act stating that nothing in the Act applies to employment performed in a workplace located in the employee's residence, removing employers from any federal safety obligations at home worksites.

The bill's own findings argue that the federal government should not require employers to interfere with an employee's home life, and that the home work environment differs from the workplaces OSHA was written for.

analysis.who_pays: Home-based employees. Work done at home would sit outside federal safety law, leaving telecommuters without OSHA standards, employer safety duties, or a federal complaint channel for hazards in their home workplace.

drawbacks.text: Employees working from home would lose the safety protections the law gives every other workplace. OSHA's standards and enforcement would simply not reach the fastest-growing category of worksite, so hazards in home offices or home workshops would have no federal oversight.
The bill does not establish any replacement protection: it creates no state, employer, or private system to cover home worksites, so the gap would be total rather than a shift to another regulator.

Supporters would argue that OSHA was never designed to reach into private homes and that applying employer obligations to a residence invades the home, a cost to employers and household privacy that an honest supporter would acknowledge; the bill's findings make this case directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: employers avoid the burden of safety compliance in spaces they do not control, and the bill's findings argue that protects household privacy. The cost falls on home workers, who lose federal safety coverage entirely with nothing replacing it. Because telecommuting was growing when the bill was introduced, carving out home worksites would exempt a widening share of work from safety law. The bill also does not distinguish between a home office used occasionally for email and a home used as a regular full-time worksite, so the exemption is broader than the privacy concern it cites.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Greg Walden introduced the bill on February 10, 2000.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, which has jurisdiction over workplace-safety law.
No cosponsors ever joined; the bill lists zero cosponsors for its entire life.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Home-based workers are better off, since federal safety law still covers work performed at home. Employers did not win the exemption they sought, and no one lost anything because the bill simply never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Home workers, who kept safety coverage

for.name: Rep. Greg Walden
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt home-based employment from the OSH Act.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never held a hearing or markup, leaving the bill to expire.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no meaningful partisan pattern ever formed; it died from inaction rather than opposition.

industries.industry: Employers with telecommuting or home-based workforces
industries.note: The bill would relieve these employers of OSHA duties for work performed in employees' homes — no standards, inspections, or enforcement at home worksites. The employer's gain is the home worker's loss of federal safety coverage, so the interests run directly against ordinary people here.
